newsitem.title: USA: Attorneys argue Swiss banks case in U.S. court.
newsitem.headline: Attorneys argue Swiss banks case in U.S. court.

text.p: Attorneys for three Swiss banks accused of hiding Holocaust-era assets argued at a U.S. court hearing on Thursday that civil lawsuits brought by the victims should be dismissed, while the victim's attorneys maintained that an investigation at least should go forward.

The case being heard by U.S. District Judge Edward Korman in Brooklyn is in the early stages, but already lawyers representing Union Bank of Switzerland, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp say the lawsuits brought by some 18,000 victims should be thrown out.
"We think class action litigation is the very worst way for all the participants to proceed," said Roger Witten, who did most of the speaking for the group representing the banks.
He called the civil action a "wasteful use of resources" and said the litigation was likely to run into large amounts of money which could be better spent on other methods of getting the assets back.
So far only 10 Holocaust victims have formally entered their names on the suit, although lawyers say they represent some 18,000 plaintiffs seeking some $20 billion in damages.
One objection to the suit cited by the bank's lawyers came from a letter written by Paul Volcker, the head of the independent committee which is also investigating hidden assets in the Swiss banks.
Referring to the Volcker letter, Witten said, "this lawsuit could actually interfere with international cooperative efforts to the point of rendering them ineffective."

Despite the investigative efforts, the victims' lawyers say not enough is being done. They argued that the investigations by the banks, the Swiss government and even the independent committee was being done "behind closed doors" and was not including the input of the victims and their families.

One reason for reluctance to back the committee and the banks' efforts, victims' lawyers argued, was that similar requests and directions to find hidden assets have not produced results. The first request for help came in 1946, with other requests coming in 1962, 1976, 1995 and 1996.
"This has been 50 years of malfeasance and misfeasance," said Arthur Miller, an attorney representing the victims. "What they are saying here is I'm taking care of it myself. Don't look at me."
Thursday's hearing addressed only some of the issues before the court. The lawyers are expected to meet with the judge again to discuss other issues before he rules, which could take weeks or months.
